definition: The dappled, shifting sunlight that filters through the leaves of trees.
exampleSentence: We lay on the moss and watched the komorebi tremble gold across our hands.
etymology: Japanese 木漏れ日, from 木 'ko' (tree) + 漏れ 'more' (leaking through) + 日 'bi' (sunlight); literally 'sunlight that leaks through trees'.

definition: The excess weight gained from comfort-eating one's way through grief or stress.
exampleSentence: Three months of breakup ice cream left him with a soft layer of kummerspeck.
etymology: German, from 'Kummer' (grief) + 'Speck' (bacon, fat); literally 'grief bacon'. Recorded in the Collins German–English Dictionary.

definition: The perfect, witty comeback that arrives only after the moment to use it has passed.
exampleSentence: Halfway down the stairs the devastating treppenwitz finally came to her, far too late.
etymology: German, from 'Treppe' (stairs) + 'Witz' (joke); a 'staircase joke', calquing the French 'esprit de l'escalier'. In the Collins German–English Dictionary.

definition: The seemingly malicious behaviour of inanimate objects that conspire to thwart us.
exampleSentence: The printer jamming five minutes before the deadline was pure resistentialism.
etymology: Coined in 1948 by humorist Paul Jennings in 'Report on Resistentialism' (The Spectator); a blend of Latin 'res' (thing) + French 'résister' + 'existentialism', spoofing Sartre. Slogan: 'Les choses sont contre nous'.

definition: The involuntary cinema of the mind that plays out vivid imagined scenes.
exampleSentence: One unread text and her kopfkino was already screening three disaster sequels.
etymology: German, from 'Kopf' (head) + 'Kino' (cinema); literally 'head cinema'.

definition: A joke so clumsily told and unfunny that you cannot help laughing anyway.
exampleSentence: His pun was such a jayus that the whole table groaned and then cracked up.
etymology: Indonesian slang; a joke whose comedic value comes precisely from its spectacular failure to be funny.

definition: The rush of joy felt on reuniting with someone after a long time apart.
exampleSentence: The airport arrivals hall was a sea of tearful retrouvailles and crushed bouquets.
etymology: French, from 'retrouver' (to find again); literally 'rediscoveries', the happiness of meeting again.

definition: The quiet certainty, on first meeting someone, that the two of you will fall in love.
exampleSentence: It wasn't love at first sight, just koi no yokan — a sense of what was coming.
etymology: Japanese 恋の予感, from 'koi' (love) + 'no' (of) + 'yokan' (premonition); the premonition of love rather than love itself.

definition: The giddy disorientation of being far from home in an unfamiliar country.
exampleSentence: The unfamiliar smells and signage filled her with a thrilling dépaysement.
etymology: French, from 'dé-' (un-) + 'pays' (country); the feeling of being 'un-countried', out of one's element.

definition: A frenzy of yearning for something impossible to attain.
exampleSentence: His nympholepsy for a vanished, idealized past kept him from ever living in the present.
etymology: From Greek 'nympholēptos', 'seized by nymphs'; the ancients believed such ecstasy struck those who glimpsed a nymph. In Merriam-Webster.

definition: A gullible person who will credulously swallow whatever they are told.
exampleSentence: Every conspiracy thread found a fresh gobemouche ready to believe and repost it.
etymology: French, from 'gober' (to gulp down) + 'mouche' (fly); literally a 'fly-swallower', mouth hanging open. In Merriam-Webster.

definition: A deep-rooted sense of honour, dignity and duty toward family and community.
exampleSentence: Out of filotimo the old fisherman refused payment for ferrying the stranded family home.
etymology: Greek φιλότιμο, from 'philos' (love) + 'timi' (honour); literally 'love of honour', a cardinal Greek virtue.

definition: Stoic inner grit that keeps you going long after reason says to quit.
exampleSentence: It took pure sisu to finish the marathon on a sprained ankle in the sleet.
etymology: Finnish, from 'sisus' (the insides, the gut); a near-mythic Finnish ideal of resolve in adversity.

definition: The intuitive art of reading a room and sensing others' unspoken moods.
exampleSentence: She had the nunchi to change the subject the instant the table went quiet.
etymology: Korean 눈치, from 'nun' (eye); literally 'eye-measure', the quick gauging of a situation through subtle cues.

definition: The gentle, bittersweet sadness felt at the fleetingness of all beautiful things.
exampleSentence: Watching the petals scatter, she was filled with mono no aware for the brief spring.
etymology: Japanese 物の哀れ, from 'mono' (things) + 'aware' (pathos); the term was central to the eighteenth-century scholar Motoori Norinaga's literary criticism.

definition: The giddy, fluttering thrill of a romantic or exciting moment.
exampleSentence: Just remembering his text gave her a fresh wave of kilig.
etymology: Tagalog; added to the Oxford English Dictionary in March 2016, its earliest cited use being 1981 in the Diliman Review.

definition: Giving confident opinions on matters well beyond one's actual knowledge.
exampleSentence: His ultracrepidarian lectures on medicine annoyed every doctor at the dinner.
etymology: From Latin 'ne ultra crepidam' ('not beyond the sandal'), the painter Apelles' rebuke to a meddling cobbler in Pliny; coined as an English word by William Hazlitt around 1819.

definition: Boldly self-confident, cheeky and a little flashily daring.
exampleSentence: The wee one strode onstage gallus as you like and belted the first note.
etymology: Scots, possibly from 'gallows' (one fit for the gallows, hence reckless); now an admiring word for swagger. In the Dictionaries of the Scots Language.

definition: Habitually gloomy, taciturn and darkly sardonic in temperament.
exampleSentence: He gave a saturnine half-smile and went back to brooding over his coffee.
etymology: From Latin 'Saturnus'; in medieval astrology, those born under the slow, cold planet Saturn were thought to be sluggish and grave.

definition: Warmly friendly, kindly and snugly comfortable, of a person or place.
exampleSentence: The wee couthie pub welcomed us in from the rain with a roaring fire.
etymology: Scots, from 'couth' (known, familiar, kindly); the opposite of the now-common 'uncouth'. In the Dictionaries of the Scots Language.

definition: Elegantly harmonious, with every part fitting neatly and gracefully together.
exampleSentence: The essay's concinnous structure made each argument slide effortlessly into the next.
etymology: From Latin 'concinnus' (skilfully put together, neat); harmony achieved through fine proportion.

definition: Given to wandering about at night.
exampleSentence: His noctivagant habits meant the city's empty 3 a.m. streets felt like home.
etymology: From Latin 'nox, noctis' (night) + 'vagari' (to wander); a night-wanderer.

definition: Spontaneously playful, done for the sheer fun of it.
exampleSentence: Her ludic doodles crept into the margins of every serious report.
etymology: From French 'ludique', from Latin 'ludus' (play, game); pertaining to undirected, joyful play.

definition: Mysteriously entrancing, as if possessing a hidden, oracular power.
exampleSentence: The cellist drew an orphic hush over the entire candlelit hall.
etymology: From Orpheus, the Greek musician whose song could charm beasts, stones and even the dead; hence mystically beautiful and spellbinding.

definition: Worn out, exhausted and feeling a bit under the weather.
exampleSentence: After the night shift she felt fair wabbit and crawled straight into bed.
etymology: Scots; an expressive word for being drained or run-down. In the Dictionaries of the Scots Language.

definition: To do nothing on purpose, idling without aim or guilt.
exampleSentence: On Sundays she simply niksens by the window, watching the street go by.
etymology: Dutch, from 'niks' (nothing); the deliberate, restorative practice of doing nothing at all.

definition: In strict confidence; secretly and off the record.
exampleSentence: The deal was negotiated sub rosa, months before any public announcement.
etymology: Latin, literally 'under the rose'; a rose hung above a meeting once signalled that all said beneath it was secret.

definition: Out in the open air at night, sleeping under the bare sky and stars.
exampleSentence: We abandoned the stuffy tent and slept à la belle étoile by the embers.
etymology: French, literally 'under the beautiful star'; spending the night outdoors with no roof but the heavens.

definition: In a secretive, muddled and disorderly fashion.
exampleSentence: The plans were drawn up hugger-mugger, and no two people agreed on them.
etymology: English, of uncertain sixteenth-century origin; long used by Shakespeare and others for furtive, confused concealment.

definition: At full gallop; headlong and at great speed.
exampleSentence: The children went tantivy down the hill the moment the gate swung open.
etymology: English, seventeenth-century, perhaps imitative of a galloping horse's hoofbeats; also a hunting cry.
